name: Marxism
info: Marxism is a political philosophy and method of analysis, originating in the works of Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels in 19th-century Germany, that sees class struggle as the driving force of history; it inspired revolutions, parties and many academic disciplines.

facts.thinkers: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, who co-developed communist theory; Karl Kautsky, who popularised the term Marxism; Eduard Bernstein, his revisionist rival; Vladimir Lenin; Rosa Luxemburg; Leon Trotsky; Joseph Stalin; Mao Zedong; Louis Althusser; Leszek Kołakowski, a critic
facts.texts: The German Ideology (1845); Theses on Feuerbach (1845); The Communist Manifesto (1848); A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy (1859); Capital; Engels’s The Condition of the Working Class in England in 1844 and Origins of the Family, Private Property, and the State (1884); Marx’s Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, published in 1932
facts.ideas: historical materialism; base and superstructure; class struggle as the force of historical change; exploitation through surplus value; alienation; class consciousness; revolution replacing capitalism with socialism and then a classless, stateless and moneyless society
facts.today: China, Cuba, Laos, North Korea and Vietnam remained the only officially Marxist–Leninist states at the turn of the 21st century; Marxist theory continues to be developed by thinkers such as David Harvey, Nancy Fraser and Silvia Federici, and shapes many academic fields

t: Marx and Engels held that a society’s mode of production is the base of its politics, law and ideas, and that class struggle drives historical change.

Marxism divided into many schools after Marx’s death; the most prominent in the 20th century was Marxism–Leninism, the official ideology of the Soviet Union and other Marxist states, while Western Marxism, libertarian Marxism and Marxist humanism often criticised state socialism.

Critics from several quarters, among them Karl Popper, Austrian economists and anarchists, attacked its predictions, its economics and its view of the state, while its concepts of alienation, exploitation and class struggle entered the social sciences and humanities.
dyk: Engels did not favour the word Marxism, and in 1882 he reported that Marx had said of the views of Paul Lafargue, a self-proclaimed Marxist, that if they were Marxist, then “one thing is certain and that is that I am not a Marxist.”
ev: Marx sets out the materialist conception of history in The German Ideology
Marx and Engels publish the 12,000-word Communist Manifesto in February
Engels publishes Origins of the Family, Private Property, and the State after Marx’s death in 1883
The Bolsheviks take power from the Russian Provisional Government in the October Revolution
Marx’s Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 appear, the birth of Marxist humanism
The People’s Republic of China is declared after the Chinese Communist Revolution
The Cuban Revolution brings Fidel Castro to power; he later adopts the Leninist model
The Soviet Union dissolves, and its constituent nations abandon Marxist–Leninist models

sections.origins:
Marxism originated in the works of the 19th-century German philosophers Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels. They first met in September 1844 and, finding that they held similar views of philosophy and socialism, collaborated on works such as Die heilige Familie (The Holy Family). After Marx was deported from France in January 1845 they moved to Belgium, which permitted greater freedom of expression than other European countries, and in January 1846 they established the Communist Correspondence Committee in Brussels.

Marx gave his account of the materialist conception of history in The German Ideology (1845) and in the preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy (1859). In 1847 the two began writing The Communist Manifesto, based on Engels’s The Principles of Communism, and published the 12,000-word pamphlet in February 1848. Belgium expelled them in March, and they moved to Cologne, where they published the radical newspaper Neue Rheinische Zeitung.

After Marx died in 1883, Engels became the editor and translator of his writings. The word Marxism was popularised by Karl Kautsky, who considered himself an orthodox Marxist in the dispute between Marx’s orthodox and revisionist followers; his rival Eduard Bernstein later adopted it too. Engels did not support the term, which he held was used as a rhetorical qualifier by those casting themselves as genuine followers of Marx.
sections.ideas:
Marxism uses a materialist methodology, later known as historical materialism, to analyse social change from the collective ways in which humans make their living. A society’s mode of production forms its economic base, and from it rise legal and political forms and a dominant ideology, the superstructure. The relation is reflexive: the superstructure acts back on the base, so that the relationship is dialectic, driven by conflicts and contradictions. When the forces of production, such as technology, outgrow the existing relations of production, Marx wrote, an era of social revolution begins. He described four stages of development in Western Europe: primitive communism, slave society, feudalism and capitalism.

Under capitalism the bourgeoisie, who own the means of production, face the proletariat, who must sell their labour power. In Marx’s theory, exploitation takes the form of surplus value, the difference between the value a worker produces and the wage received, and the worker’s entry into employment is voluntary only in appearance, since the worker must work or starve. Alienation, the estrangement of people from their humanity, is in his view a systematic result of capitalism.

Marxists expect the state, seen as a weapon of one class over another, to be seized by working-class revolution and eventually to wither away, leaving a classless society. Marx himself used socialism and communism interchangeably; the distinction as two stages entered Marxism after his death.
sections.spread:
Since Marx’s death his ideas have been elaborated and adapted by many thinkers and movements, so that there is no single, definitive Marxist theory. The failure of the 1905 Russian Revolution, and of socialist movements to resist the outbreak of the First World War, led to renewed theoretical work by Lenin and Rosa Luxemburg on Marx’s crisis theory and on imperialism. Kautsky and Bernstein stood on opposite sides of the dispute between orthodox and revisionist followers.

After the October Revolution of 1917 the Bolsheviks founded the first socialist state, and in 1919 the Soviet government set up the Communist Academy and the Marx–Engels–Lenin Institute for doctrinal study. Lenin’s death in 1924 opened a struggle between Stalin and Trotsky over the interpretation of Marxist and Leninist theory, and this period is marked by the development of Marxism–Leninism as the dominant strain. Marxist humanism was born in 1932 with the publication of Marx’s early manuscripts, and Western Marxism was accepted within Western academia in the 1940s.

In China the Communist Party, founded in 1921, took power in 1949, and Mao Zedong developed a Marxism for China built on the peasantry, New Democracy, the mass line and people’s war. The Cuban Revolution followed in 1959. Further schools include Austro-Marxism, council communism, Eurocommunism, Trotskyism, Luxemburgism, Marxist feminism and libertarian Marxism.
sections.power:
With the October Revolution of 1917 the Bolsheviks took power, founding the first socialist state. They promised to end Russian involvement in the First World War, and Lenin’s government instituted universal education, universal healthcare and expanded women’s rights. After the revolution the Soviet government fought the White Movement and several independence movements in the Russian Civil War.

After Lenin’s death Marxism–Leninism became the official ideology of the Soviet Union and of other Marxist states. Under Stalin, Soviet archaeology was reformed on Marxist lines and criticised as inherently bourgeois, and Marxist historiography suffered as the government demanded overdetermined historical writing; the History of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (Bolsheviks), published in the 1930s, was written to justify the nature of Bolshevik party life under Stalin.

In China the People’s Republic was declared in 1949, and from 1966 to 1976 the Maoist government carried out the Cultural Revolution to purge Chinese society of capitalist elements. After Mao’s death Deng Xiaoping revised or abandoned many of its policies and encouraged privatised industry. Castro adopted the Leninist model in Cuba and allied with the Soviet Union. In the late 1980s and early 1990s most of the states that had professed Marxism–Leninism collapsed: Gorbachev’s reforms, together with rising ethnic nationalism, led to the Soviet Union’s dissolution in late 1991, and its successor nations abandoned Marxist–Leninist models, most converting to capitalist economies.
sections.critiques:
Criticism has come from many ideologies and disciplines: alleged lack of internal consistency, historical determinism, the suppression of individual rights, difficulties in implementing communism, and economic problems such as distorted or absent price signals and reduced incentives. Karl Popper held that Marxism was at first scientific because Marx made predictions, but that when they were not borne out the theory avoided falsification through ad hoc hypotheses and degenerated into pseudoscientific dogma. Leszek Kołakowski wrote that Marx’s theory was incomplete or ambiguous in many places and could be applied in contradictory ways, and judged some laws of dialectics to be truisms, dogmas or nonsense.

Critics also point to the absence of worsening crises that overthrow capitalism and to revolutions occurring in undeveloped regions rather than the most advanced capitalist nations. The claim that Marxist states had lower living standards than capitalist ones has been disputed. Dmitriev and Bortkiewicz alleged internal inconsistency in Marx’s value theory, and Okishio’s theorem casts doubt on the falling rate of profit; Austrian economists such as Böhm-Bawerk and Mises attacked the law of value and the possibility of socialist economic calculation.

Anarchists such as Mikhail Bakunin criticised Marx’s authoritarian bent, and libertarian and classical liberal economists argue that the lack of free markets leads to authoritarianism. Among Marxists, Alex Callinicos accused Western Marxists of making conceptual clarification an end in itself.
sections.legacy:
Marxism stands as one of the most influential and controversial intellectual traditions in modern history. It has inspired revolutions, social movements and parties across the world, and concepts such as alienation, exploitation and class struggle have become part of the social sciences and humanities. It has shaped fields including anthropology, archaeology, economics, historiography, literary criticism, sociology, education and political science. A 2007 survey of American professors by Neil Gross and Solon Simmons found that 17.6% of social science professors and 5.0% of humanities professors identified as Marxists.

Marxian economics, though considered heterodox, has contributed to mainstream understanding of the global economy, and some concepts, such as creative destruction, have been fitted for use in capitalist systems. British Marxist historians such as Christopher Hill, E. P. Thompson and Eric Hobsbawm developed history from below, and the Frankfurt School combined some Marxist concepts with the ideas of Max Weber. Because of its former state-supported position, Marxist thought met a backlash in post-communist states such as Poland, while it remains prominent in sociological research sanctioned by Communist-ruled states such as China.

At the turn of the 21st century China, Cuba, Laos, North Korea and Vietnam remained the only officially Marxist–Leninist states. Marxist theory has continued to develop in the work of David Harvey, Nancy Fraser, Erik Olin Wright, Silvia Federici and others.

summary: Marxism is a materialist philosophy and method of analysis that Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels developed in 19th-century Germany, centred on class struggle and the critique of capitalism. It split into many schools, the most prominent being Marxism–Leninism, and it shaped revolutions, states and academic disciplines.

George Lichtheim, Marxism: An Historical and Critical Study (Routledge, 2015)
Shlomo Avineri, The Social and Political Thought of Karl Marx (Cambridge University Press, 1968)

David McLellan, Marxism After Marx (Palgrave Macmillan, 2007)
notes: Start 1848 (the Communist Manifesto, the first work the article names as setting out communist theory with its famous opening line); the article dates The German Ideology to 1845 and the Marx–Engels meeting to 1844. circa false by choice.

The article says little about Marxist states' record in power: it names the Cultural Revolution (1966-1976) and Soviet scholarly regimentation but gives no figures for purges, famines or camps, so none are stated; the editor may wish to link to Marxism–Leninism, Stalinism and Maoism profiles for those.

The Western Marxism, Rosa Luxemburg and Marxist–Leninist ‘Schools’ subsections are empty or nearly empty in the saved text. Left out: the 'Marxist education' list of names, Sayyid Qutb's quoted criticism (religious critique, short), the aesthetics and literary criticism detail.
The 1991 event: the article says 'late 1991'; the 1932 event label is the manuscripts' publication; 1949 and 1959 are from the Chinese Revolution and Late 20th century sections.
Ideas text: 'primitive communism … capitalism' stages are the article's list of four for Western Europe; the article hedges that Marx did not claim a master key to history (not included for length).
Gross and Simmons survey figures are the article's 2007 survey; kept as a dated fact, not a ranking.
Left out of critiques for length: Acemoglu and Robinson's charge that Marx's economics ignored institutions, disputed by John Roemer and Nicholas Vrousalis.
